positions/pentecostal-initial-evidence/a: Baptism in the Holy Spirit with the evidence of tongues
positions/pentecostal-initial-evidence/o: Baptism in the Holy Spirit is an experience distinct from and subsequent to conversion, empowering for witness, whose initial physical evidence is speaking in tongues.
positions/pentecostal-initial-evidence/c: Every believer should seek the baptism in the Holy Spirit as promised in Acts 1:5–8 and 2:38–39.
This baptism is distinct from, and normally subsequent to, regeneration.
Its initial physical evidence is speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gives utterance (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6).
Its purpose is power for witness and service, not salvation.
All the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 are for today.
positions/pentecostal-initial-evidence/o: Building on Wesleyan and Holiness teaching on a "second blessing" and on Reformed "higher life" Spirit-baptism (Keswick, R. A. Torrey), Charles F. Parham at Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Kansas, concluded that tongues were the biblical evidence; Agnes Ozman spoke in tongues on 1 January 1901. William J. Seymour carried the teaching to Azusa Street, Los Angeles (1906). The Assemblies of God enshrined "initial physical evidence" in its Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916).
positions/pentecostal-initial-evidence/s: In Acts, whenever the outpouring of the Spirit is described in detail (Acts 2, 10, 19), tongues accompany it, and in Acts 10:46 tongues is how Peter’s companions knew the Spirit had been given.
Acts 8 and 19 show believers who had received Christ but not yet the Spirit’s empowering, supporting subsequence.
It provides a clear, objective sign that encourages believers to seek empowerment, and its fruit is visible in the extraordinary missionary expansion of Pentecostalism.
Paul’s rhetorical question "do all speak with tongues?" expects the answer no (1 Cor 12:30).
Narrative texts in Acts describe what happened, not necessarily what must always happen; Acts 8 mentions no tongues.
Paul says all believers were baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Cor 12:13), suggesting Spirit-baptism is conversion-initiation (James Dunn, Baptism in the Holy Spirit, 1970).
Even Seymour later came to regard tongues alone as an insufficient evidence, stressing love; many Pentecostals in Chile, Germany and elsewhere never accepted the doctrine.
positions/pentecostal-initial-evidence/r: Pentecostals distinguish the "gift of tongues" for public ministry (not all have it, 1 Cor 12:30) from the "sign of tongues" accompanying Spirit baptism (available to all).
They argue that Luke is a theologian in his own right whose narratives teach a distinct pneumatology of empowerment (Roger Stronstad, 1984), not merely Paul’s soteriology.
Contemporary Pentecostal theologians (Macchia) reframe tongues as a sacramental sign of the Spirit’s presence rather than a mechanical test.
positions/pentecostal-initial-evidence/c: Became the defining doctrine of classical Pentecostal denominations (Assemblies of God, Church of God, Pentecostal Holiness Church, Foursquare).
Drew a sharp line between Pentecostals and both Holiness churches and fundamentalists, who largely rejected the movement.
Contributed to the Oneness ("New Issue") split of 1916 and later debates within charismatic renewal about whether tongues are necessary.
Fuelled vigorous mission in Africa, Latin America and Asia.
positions/charismatic-renewal/oneLine: Pentecostal-style experience of the Spirit and the gifts, embraced within the historic denominations without leaving them and usually without the initial-evidence doctrine.
positions/charismatic-renewal/coreClaims: The baptism or "release" of the Spirit renews faith, worship and mission within existing churches.
All the gifts, including tongues, prophecy and healing, are available today.
Tongues are common but not required as evidence.
Renewal should serve the unity and sacramental life of the Church rather than create new denominations.
In Catholic and Anglican interpretation, "baptism in the Spirit" actualises grace already given in baptism and confirmation.
positions/charismatic-renewal/origin: In 1960 Dennis Bennett, rector of St Mark’s Episcopal Church, Van Nuys, California, told his congregation he had spoken in tongues, and the renewal spread through Episcopalians, Lutherans (Larry Christenson), Presbyterians, Baptists and, after a retreat at Duquesne University in February 1967, Roman Catholics. Michael Harper’s Fountain Trust (1964) spread it in Britain. Cardinal Suenens’ Malines Documents (1974) and Paul VI’s address of 1975 gave Catholic recognition.
positions/charismatic-renewal/strongestA: It brings renewed devotion, Scripture reading and evangelism to people who remain in sacramental and liturgical churches, demonstrating that charisms and institutions need not compete.
It has strong ecumenical fruit, bringing Catholics and Protestants together in prayer and worship.
Patristic and liturgical sources (Kilian McDonnell and George Montague, Christian Initiation and Baptism in the Holy Spirit, 1991) suggest that charisms were originally part of Christian initiation.
positions/charismatic-renewal/strongestO: Critics fear it creates a two-tier membership of "Spirit-filled" and ordinary Christians, dividing congregations.
Cessationists and some confessional Lutherans see it as importing subjective experience over Word and sacrament.
Some Pentecostals regard its rejection of initial evidence and its tolerance of Catholic doctrine (e.g. Marian devotion) as compromise.
positions/charismatic-renewal/responses/: Charismatic leaders insist that all baptised Christians have the Spirit and that renewal is about releasing what is already given, not a superior class.
Church authorities have provided pastoral oversight (e.g. Catholic National Service Committees; Anglican guidelines) to keep renewal integrated with parish life.
positions/charismatic-renewal/consequenc: The Catholic Charismatic Renewal is estimated to have touched well over 100 million Catholics, especially in Latin America, Africa and the Philippines (El Shaddai).
Transformed Protestant worship through "contemporary worship" music.
Helped spawn independent charismatic churches and networks when renewal was rejected locally.
Created new ecumenical bridges (e.g. Catholic–Pentecostal dialogue since 1972).
positions/third-wave/altNames/0: Third Wave of the Holy Spirit
positions/third-wave/oneLine: Evangelicals can expect "signs and wonders" (healing, prophecy, deliverance) as part of normal kingdom ministry without adopting Pentecostal second-blessing doctrine or labels.
positions/third-wave/coreClaims/0: Spirit baptism occurs at conversion; subsequent "fillings" empower ministry.
positions/third-wave/coreClaims/1: Healing, words of knowledge and deliverance are normal tools of evangelism ("power evangelism").
positions/third-wave/coreClaims/2: Kingdom theology: the kingdom has already broken in (Ladd), so signs of it should accompany preaching.
positions/third-wave/coreClaims/3: Every believer can "do the stuff" Jesus did, not only specially gifted leaders.
positions/third-wave/origin: The term was coined by C. Peter Wagner of Fuller Theological Seminary (1983) for a "third wave" after Pentecostalism and the charismatic renewal. John Wimber, a former Quaker musician and church-growth consultant, taught the course MC510 "Signs, Wonders and Church Growth" at Fuller (1982) and led the Association of Vineyard Churches.
positions/third-wave/strongestArguments/: It integrates spiritual gifts with mainstream evangelical theology rather than requiring a two-stage experience.
Missionary anthropologists (Kraft) argue that in many cultures "power encounters" are central to conversion, as in the New Testament.
Its kingdom framework is rooted in respected biblical scholarship (Ladd).
positions/third-wave/strongestObjections: Critics argue that its claimed healings were seldom medically verified and that pragmatic church-growth logic drove it.
The Kansas City Prophets controversy (1990) and Toronto Blessing (1994) raised questions about discernment and manifestations.
Cessationists and some Pentecostals say it blurs biblical distinctions while adopting charismatic practice.
positions/third-wave/responses/0: Wimber publicly admitted mistakes (e.g. with the Kansas City Prophets) and the Vineyard disassociated from Toronto in 1995, showing willingness to self-correct.
positions/third-wave/responses/1: Advocates point to the evangelistic fruit and humility-focused "naturally supernatural" ministry style.
positions/third-wave/consequences/0: Vineyard worship music shaped global evangelical worship.
positions/third-wave/consequences/1: Brought charismatic practice into many evangelical churches without Pentecostal labels.
positions/third-wave/consequences/2: Wagner’s later work led into the New Apostolic Reformation.
positions/new-apostolic-reformation/oneL: God is restoring the offices of apostle and prophet to govern the Church and lead it to transform society, in what C. Peter Wagner called a "Second Apostolic Age".
positions/new-apostolic-reformation/core: The five-fold ministry of Ephesians 4:11 (apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers) continues, including governing apostles.
Apostles lead relational networks rather than denominations; prophets receive revelation for strategy.
Strategic-level spiritual warfare against territorial spirits advances the kingdom.
Many adherents embrace a "Seven Mountains Mandate" to influence family, religion, education, media, arts and entertainment, business and government.
A coming great harvest and transformation of nations are prophesied.
positions/new-apostolic-reformation/orig: Named by C. Peter Wagner in the mid-1990s (popularised in Churchquake!, 1999), building on the Latter Rain movement (1948), Third Wave and the global rise of independent apostolic networks, especially in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Wagner founded the International Coalition of Apostles (1999) and dated the "Second Apostolic Age" from 2001. The Seven Mountains idea is traced to Loren Cunningham and Bill Bright (1975) and was developed by Lance Wallnau and Johnny Enlow.
positions/new-apostolic-reformation/prop: Bill Johnson (Bethel Church; rejects the label)
positions/new-apostolic-reformation/stro: Ephesians 4:11–13 gives the five ministries "till we all come in the unity of the faith", implying they continue until maturity is reached.
Network-based apostolic leadership fits rapidly growing churches in the Global South better than inherited denominations.
It recovers a vision of the gospel transforming every sphere of life, not only private piety.
Most traditions hold that apostles in the foundational sense (witnesses of the risen Christ, Acts 1:21–22; 1 Cor 15:8) were unrepeatable, laid once as the Church’s foundation (Eph 2:20).
Critics (Geivett and Pivec, 2014) charge it with authoritarianism, lack of accountability and new extra-biblical revelation.

Seven Mountains and dominion theology are criticised as a form of Christian nationalism, and prominent prophets’ failed predictions (e.g. Donald Trump’s re-election in 2020) damaged credibility; some, like Jeremiah Johnson, publicly apologised.
Pentecostal denominations, including the Assemblies of God (2000 position paper on apostles and prophets), warn against its claims.
positions/new-apostolic-reformation/resp: Advocates distinguish the twelve foundational apostles from ongoing "functional" apostles who plant and oversee churches, a sense used for Barnabas and others (Acts 14:14).
Leaders such as Bill Johnson disown the NAR label and the most authoritarian forms; adherents say it is a loose, diverse network, not a single organisation.
positions/new-apostolic-reformation/cons: Shaped large independent charismatic networks globally and much of charismatic political activism in the US and Brazil.
Contributed to the "prophetic" politics of the 2016–2024 US elections and the January 2021 Capitol rally rhetoric, prompting sharp critique from fellow charismatics.
Spurred renewed debate on apostolic authority and prophetic accountability.
